html:
From 1201 to 2008 Nepal was ruled by kings: first the Mallas of the Kathmandu valley, then the Shahs of Gorkha.

The Malla kings ruled the valley from 1201. Its Newar people were farmers, craftsmen and traders on the route between India and Tibet, and for a time they minted Tibet's coins. King Jayasthiti Malla, in the late 14th century, set down rules of caste for the valley's Hindus and Buddhists alike.

After 1482 the valley split into three kingdoms: Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, each a few kilometres from the next. Their kings competed in building. The palace squares, with brick temples under tiered roofs and carved wooden windows, date mostly from these centuries.

In 1768 and 1769 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha conquered all three and founded the present country (see Nepal). His heirs expanded until the Anglo-Nepalese War.

In 1846 a courtier, Jung Bahadur Rana, killed his rivals in one night and made the office of prime minister hereditary in his family. The Ranas ruled for a century while the kings stayed in the palace. A revolt backed by India restored the king in 1951.

Parliament came in 1990 and the civil war in 1996. The monarchy was abolished on 28 May 2008.
sum: From 1201 to 2008 Nepal was ruled by kings: first the Mallas of the Kathmandu valley, then the Shahs of Gorkha.
